en: "By this sudden outpouring of the nectar-like juice from her lips, which rival the luster of the bandhūka flower, our obsession with the ambrosia has been diminished.

Homage to you, whose belly is filled with the liquid of turmeric; who stands upon the mere tip of the tongue; who is other than Truth itself; who is a manifest thief in the plundering of wealth; who possesses the great scholarship of describing wretched forms and colors; who is the foremost of deceits; and who is the womb of the brothel of passion. JMu_2.

That meditation which is always directed toward the Supreme Lord; that mind which is free from passion; that action which is extremely firm, terrible, and profound for the sake of prosperity; that great reverence;

and even that wondrous gift of one's body performed without any sense of transformation—that is found only in a courtesan who is an ascetic in the Kali Age, for the world has been permeated by her nature.

She bears the wealthy upon her head, creates universal delusion with ease, and maintains a partiality for the courtesan’s quarter incessantly; she is never satisfied even with those who are not mixed [with the low-born], she desires to drink the blood of everyone, and like the form of Garuḍa, she still does not rest in her practice of devouring snakes—that is, the paramour. // JMu_4 //
Let those fools dwell in the city of the Gandharvas and enjoy the wealth acquired in their dreams; let them even fashion the beauty of garlands from flowers of the sky for a moment.
Having obtained the favor of courtesans—which is like the breaking of a rabbit’s horn—those fools sit at ease, solely for the purpose of exhausting all their possessions. Ah! JMu_5.

"O friend, first instill whiteness in soot, transfer fickleness to the troops of monkeys, produce straightness in a bow, and fashion softness in a mass of stones; achieve sweetness in the neem tree, establish fragrance in garlic, and cultivate affection even for a group of courtesans—only after that, my friend, will you see [the impossible]. JMu_6 //
If Time were devoted to compassion; if the Kali age were fond of Dharma today; if the sword were gentle; if the serpent were a giver of contentment;

if fire were exceedingly cool; if the wicked person were a benefactor to all; if poison were to become life-giving; and if even a courtesan were to be in love with him—[then perhaps there would be such a thing]. (JMu 7)

A fool, a man free from vice, a merchant, a king’s official free from deceit, a pure person, a servant under one’s own control, a dullard, one devoted to virtue, a thief devoid of desire, a fearful man, one of peaceful mind, a wealthy man, a humble person, a slanderer, and a righteous man—could any such person ever anywhere at any time be truly enamored with a courtesan? (JMu 8)
Desire does not exist in one who is terrified; shamelessness exists not in a group of unchaste women; there is no water in mirages, nor is there any constancy in prosperity;

dharma does not exist in an atheist; wealth does not exist for one whose mind is intoxicated by negligence; and generally, not even a single drop of affection exists in the world of courtesans. (JMu 9)
That absolute affection which exists between a horse and its rider, between a mongoose and a venomous snake, between a cat and mice,
and which is slowly recognized among lovers when wealth is exhausted, when kinsmen are distressed, and when public scandal is firm— that very same affection is innate to the class of courtesans.

Behold: whatever was ordained for Yudhiṣṭhira by means of dice, or what Viṣṇu did to Bali, or what Śukra did to the Lord of Wealth (Kubera), or even what Kali did to King Nala—all that, having gathered together and churned the ocean with the combined forces of gods and asuras, this courtesan performs effortlessly in the houses of lovers.

Know that for a talkative man, the limit of battle is the mouth; for a family, the limit is the birth of a wicked son; for kinship, the limit is the ground of dispute; for happiness, the limit is the end of learning;

for the eloquent, the limit is the assembly of the wise; for a vow, the limit is fickleness; for bondage, know that the limit is the exhaustion of wealth; and for passion for a courtesan, the limit is the same.

A master regards one who has sought refuge as if he were cruel; a mature yogi regards a worldly man like a perfected soul regards a transmigrator; a pure brahmin regards an outcaste; a prosperous country regards a leper;
a noble family-man regards a haughty son of a slave-girl; and a wealthy man regards a petitioner. At the end, courtesans look upon a penniless person as if he were mere straw.

A Brahmin is satisfied by sacrificial fees and great gifts; a servant by the rising of clouds; a farmer by [the success of his crops]; a bad counselor by calamities; a hero by hundreds of rash acts; a hunter by wild animals;

a bard by those who are generous; a father by the excellence of his offspring; a merchant by excessive profits; a physician by those afflicted with disease; and a courtesan by masters of pregnant women.

The ignorant man plays with quarrels; the courtier with elegant verses; the debtor with his debts; the fowler with living birds; the gambler with dice; Yama with living beings; the village headman with his subjects; the master with his servants; the child with balls; and likewise, the courtesan plays with young men who are ever-new, as she does with her sons and her wealth. JMu_15 //
A servant is quickly cast down by service to a wicked master; a king by his own arbitrary misconduct; a poet by vanity; one of noble birth by the fire of anger;
an ascetic by being greedy for special enjoyments; a sick man by eating unwholesome food; and a passionate man by frequenting the women of the crossroads.
He was a swarm of locusts to the rice fields, a host of woodworms to the towering growth of bamboo, a rutting elephant to the lotus pond, a fierce wind to the flower garden,
the sun’s own brother to the orb of the moon, a submarine fire to the ocean, and a lowly harlot to the wealth of lovers— a pestilence in the form of a wedge.

O brother, excessive boasting of one's heroism, bowing before enemies for one's pride, bad character for one's beauty, fickleness when elevated by success, the grip of arrogance for one's knowledge, moral corruption for one's power, and garrulousness for one's excellence in learning— these are the ways a courtesan corrupts everything with her deceptive charms.

He who desires shade from the clouds through wicked men, goodness from the noble through begging, greatness of honor through wretchedness, fame through the arts of rogues, friendship through servility,
happiness through indulgence, dharma through the slaughter of living beings, wealth through the grace of gambling, and luxury through courtesans— he is merely a bull in human form.

There is no blindness equal to folly; no suffering equal to that of a servant; no disease equal to consumption (yakṣman); no mental anguish equal to that caused by a wicked son; no terror equal to that of a dependent;

no hardship equal to the journey on a road; no enemy equal to the senses; no misfortune equal to another’s wife; nothing is seen to be more inevitably blameworthy than a life of short duration, nor is anything seen equal to a courtesan.
Is even a crow a bird? Is even a desert a place? Is even a *karīra* tree a branching tree? Is even Rāhu a planet? And could even a camel be a vehicle?
Is even glass a gem? Is even a deer an elephant? Or is even a servant a human being? Is even a courtesan a graceful woman? And is he who is attached to her truly a lover? // JMu_21 //
What is that action which destroys happiness? That tongue which is not piercing.

What is that love which is unstable? He who is devoid of virtue. What is that prosperity which does not deserve enjoyment? He who does not know the difference between people. Is there any dalliance with courtesans that is artificial? [Indeed, all such things are artificial. JMu_22 //

Far away are those riches in which the tarnishing of one's honor arises; let that friend be happy whose mouth is full of honey but whose heart is full of deceit. May those enjoyments come to an end by any means through the violation of propriety—better even than sexual union with prostitutes for a price, which leads to death at some point.

The misplaced attachment of the Lord of Passion (Kāma), the violation of propriety for love, the futility of fresh youth, a certain sprout of blemish upon affection, the disregard for good fortune, the lack of merit in the splendor of beauty’s essence, a mockery of erotic sentiment—what more can be said? It is merely the ostentation of a courtesan's pleasure.
He whose mind is agitated by passion, who has been deceived by his own youth, and who has been gazed upon with side-long glances that are the very faces of misfortune;
he who has abandoned all consideration of what is proper or improper—that lustful worm indeed finds delight in the great neem tree known as the hips of courtesans.

This must be some great curse; such is the ripening of evil deeds; this is the supreme wickedness of Fate; this is Misfortune herself manifest—since, having abandoned a woman of noble family, young men serve a multitude of courtesans, forsaking both affection, constancy, love, and their husbands.
Even contact with them is exceedingly harsh; even the mere appearance of intimacy brings no prosperity; even a glance causes despair; even a single conversation is a source of corruption.

Even their shadow is deceptive in nature, and even the wafting of their perfume is like deadly *hālāhala* poison. What then can be said of attachment to courtesans? Oh, it is a great act of recklessness!

Deceit is its father, the sixty-four arts its mothers, and the theft of wealth—wherein every word is false—is its primary vow; its very limbs are for sale, and the bodiless God of Love himself is its companion. What medicine is there for this plague of the courtesan, which consists of hundreds of calamities?

The female vulture is intent upon meat; the fierce bee upon the abundance of honey; the female serpent upon the manner of biting with sharp claws; the minnow upon rolling on its back; and the mouse upon the pretext of wealth. Thus, the courtesan stands in this world through many forms for the sake of deceiving her lovers.
Sovereignty consists of consuming honey, meat, fish, and crocodiles; the minister is an old procuress; the one to be punished is the son of a merchant-leader; lovers are penniless servants;
conduct is the giving of many curses; the lowest friend is wealth; life is for courtesans; and the beloved is ruined by wandering through the city. JMu_30 //

"He is a man of passion," "He is a man of right conduct," "He has attained the most venerable state," "He is worthy of praise," "He is addicted to vice," "He is of low birth," "He is the foremost of family men," "He is honorable," "He is a victim of misfortune," "Oh, he is a rogue! "He is a trusted friend"—or what more could be said? In every possible condition, the man of authority is thus honored by courtesans.

O libertine, that brothel which you behold before you with supreme devotion—a place reeking of the smell of cooking meat and potent liquor, crowded with maidservants and actresses—is where the household deity resides: the procuress, who performs a ritual striking of the quarters, for whom there is a daily offering of oblations consisting of herds of animal-like wealthy lovers.

The supreme duty of the world of courtesans consists of offering their own bodies, performing charming and flattering services, making requests appropriate to their affection, and seeking audiences at the windows of the wealthy. (On *māṃspāka*, see Pāṇini 6.1.144: *aparasaparāḥ kriyāsātatye*.)
Furthermore, for a courtesan, this [act] is exceedingly intense; therein lies the vow of Agastya, wherein a single offering of one's life is made by all lovers who are like oceans of jewels.

O lustful men! On the broad slabs of the hips of courtesans—which are beautified by rows of folds set as sureties for Kandarpa, and which are struck by the falling nooses of their arms gracefully raised in play—whatever sport you have indulged in here with dice-like side-glances will yield as its only future reward nothing but poverty.

"Today I died by the spear; today my life was born; today my vow must be fulfilled; there is no renunciant superior to him"—thus you will soon hear the words of the harsh courtesan, who praises her rival and says, "That prince does not desire me; he knows only that she is my mother," like the speech of a deluded serpent.

She reveals her impurity, spreads dense worthlessness, and—alas!—inflicts blame even upon a worthy recipient; like the flame of a lamp at night, the prostitute shines forth, and therein this swarm of men, blinded by the delusion of her beauty, brings about its own downfall like moths falling into a fire. Alas, alas! What a multitude of serpents!
Intent on the act of pulling hair, robbing others of their vigor, spreading a certain languor while her face bears a smile, and clinging to the side of the ear;
causing trembling and confusion of mind in young men, she is slowly censured as the reproach of youth—the prostitute is seen. (JMu 37)

This merciless method of crushing with the teeth, produced with such delight through the application of wit and forceful, relentless squeezing of the arms like a mechanical press—it is by means of this that the courtesans extract the supreme essence from the lover, who is as succulent as sugarcane; they take his core, while merely casting him out like the husks.
Scolding with words such as "wood-chip" or "splinter," seizing garments and other items, striking with fists, and furthermore, looking at her with averted eyes, insulting her, or even kicking her—
whatever such things she previously observed during the course of the bold advances of lovers in dalliance, all that the courtesan performs for them when they are being expelled.

The frequent kissing, the repeated embracing of all limbs, the longing gaze, the impetuous utterance of flatteries, the talk of sincere affection, and whatever entreaties are made in secret—all these things of courtesans are like poison; they must always be considered with great skill by those who desire love.

Those on this earth who understand the deception in the gestures of the buttocks, the delusion in the various playings of the eyebrows, the crookedness in the nail-marks, the artifice in the methods of lovemaking,
the falsehood within the sounds of "sīt," and the theft of wealth everywhere— they alone are the truly wise regarding the supreme secret of courtesans.

Courtesans open the gates for the expenditure of wealth by lovers through the arrival of guests, through various elaborate social diversions, through the sequence of festivals and the lunar days of spring, through the rising of anger and favor, and through various longings for gold, jewels, garments, and sensual objects.
A guest, wealth, being pampered by one's father, association with a circle of libertines, self-conceit, youth, residence in a city, a fickle mind regarding the science of love,
music, the night, the moon, intoxication from wine, and rivalry with co-wives— all these provide assistance to courtesans in seizing the wealth of those who are infatuated with them.
Set aside your cleverness; your skill in the arts is obscured by your actions, and your goodness has vanished. What else can be said?

Even a heap of virtues is fruitless, O libertine, for that courtesan is not satisfied by affection, nor by prostrations, nor by love, nor by pleasing gestures, nor even by one's life—unless it be with wealth. JMu_44.
"O Master, I am indeed your slave; all wealth belongs to you. Do not, O merciless one, abandon me who stands here! Without you, I consider the entire world to be empty.
When the prostitute weeps suddenly before her paramour after saying this, only those know that she is merely crying for the wealth of a poor man who has enjoyed her leftovers.

"Remembering someone in a dream, you were seen by me as my beloved; therefore, why do you now thus deceive me without cause? It would be better for me to remain awake during the nights, for even sleep is my enemy"—by such words, what lover can be trusted by a group of courtesans?

With her eyebrows so excessively arched, with her hair-locks curled at the ends, and with the corners of her eyes straightened by various gestures as if indifferent, that wretched courtesan constantly displays her own fickle mental disposition to young men; yet, being utterly foolish, they do not understand it.
"First with indirect speech, then with indifference, and after that, one must give much; there, I shall go so that our meeting may happen again"—
even when addressed thus, if the lover is poor, dull-witted, and attached, he does not understand despite the many words of the maidservants, and is then warded off by the bolts of their hands.

Furthermore, when he sees that wealth has been acquired by him through the power of time, his lover—my dear one—becomes angry, and a quarrel arises with his mother, who says, "He was sent away by you.

Then, having undertaken vows and the like toward him and feigning her own separation from him, another reconciliation is subsequently brought about between them by means of the courtesans acting as intermediaries.

"O mature one, giver of life, handsome lord, noble, generous, and dear one! Without you, what is the use of wealth, what is the use of a house, or even these very vital breaths?"—to him who was thus addressed, that harlot now feels no shame, but instead reproaches him, saying: "O hopeless, wretched beast, go away now; shame on you, a penniless rogue! Thus she speaks with humiliation.
Some became gamblers, some became beggars, some became servants, others laborers for the wealthy, and some became flatterers;
with rags draped over their shoulders,
these former lovers of courtesans— now rendered powerless by grief— became the attendants of those very women.

A base man, rendered helpless by courtesans, becomes impoverished; fallen into the vice of gambling, he loses his very self through that misfortune. Besieged by gamblers, he becomes distressed and commits theft; then, as a thief, he becomes liable to execution by the king. Alas! The end resulting from attachment to sense-objects is truly miserable.
Their livelihood consists of the art of feigned passion; it is not ill-conduct that is their fault, nor does widowhood oppress them, for there is a reversal in the estimation of the good and the bad.
In doing whatever they please and in seizing the property of others, shame brings them no pain, nor is there fear of the king—alas, with what ease courtesans live!
A woman is delightful at first, but in the end she is nothing but deadly poison; this is indeed a calamity for everyone, and it is especially so in the case of a courtesan.
Therefore, she has been described primarily as such, and the collection of virtues and faults explained in connection with her should also be reflected upon with care.
The snares of the wild beasts of the mind— terrible with the tenfold expansion of passion—
are like the surging floods of ocean waves;
they have been produced neither by the surrender of a master, nor, O friend, by friendship.
Or else, through conflict, women are to be protected from the transgressions of those who are secretive, introverted, and reckless.

Alas, this practice of gambling—a mere pretense of the great vow of the ash-bath, performed by those whose fortune has already declined; consisting of the artful skill of palmistry and the sleight-of-hand of total denial; characterized by the repeated theft of one's hopes and a hatred for the world; a source of dispute and an invitation to poverty—fie upon it! What more can be said? JMu_56 //
Is even hunting to be practiced by the wise? For it is a ground for cruel acts of violence, a mother to manifold negligence, and its burden is the lack of purposeful activity;

it is frequented by base village dogs, and its qualities—such as dwelling in empty forests, constant wandering, and physical exertion—are fruitless and false, resulting only in the exhaustion of the body.
Excluding purity, conduct, and reflection; acting as a teacher of all improper and harmful practices; shattering various secret and hidden mantras; a darkness for the eyes that knows no night;
acting like a demon through the various intoxications of speech, dice, and negligence—this embodied, impure liquor is dear to whom else but another [such as this]?

Tell me, how can that wicked speaker himself still live—his harsh and evil speech, which is like a falling meteor, a companion to the fierce winds of summer storms, made into a domestic servant by the hollows of the *garu* trees cherished on Shiva’s neck, and which is a constant friend to the saw upon the tip of his tongue? Alas! How does he survive?
Imposing fierce punishment upon his subjects all of a sudden, acting like Yama, and delighting in the misappropriation and ruin of wealth, he was a traitor to himself;

whereas Kamalākara—who is gentle, who acts with gentleness, who is the joy of the eyes of the entire world, who is worthy of being celebrated by the virtuous, and who is endowed with prosperity—alas, what splendor does he not deserve?

Instruction for the virtuous is the Great Lord of cyclic existence, the sun for darkness, the physician for diseases, the atonement for sin, the scripture for ignorance, water for thirst, the perfected command for poison, the refuge of sacred sites for the infirmity of old age, and the means for pacifying the host of calamities affecting the seven constituents of sovereignty. (JMu 61)
The syllable *oṃ* is the pinnacle of hardships; the discernment of one's own virtues is the source of pleasures; occasional application is the kinsman of skill in all forms of learning;

the ultimate limit of miseries is the merchant’s pursuit of worldly travel for the sake of wealth; and it is the gateway to another birth for living beings—enough of this prolixity; farewell to foreign lands!

Even though there exists another region, vast and noble, filled with various commentaries abounding in detailed and wondrous tales and possessing faultless, charming conduct— nevertheless, my friend, it is beautiful that within one’s own home there flows a continuous stream of the essence of speech, made grand by assemblies of virtuous men.
Worthy of worship are those from whose lotus-like mouths the fragrant exhalations of Sarasvatī waft forth in syllables as sweet as drops of *makaranda* honey;
and worthy of worship also are those who fall within that interval, partaking of the grace of bees, who perceive this world as permeated by intense bliss and both praise and censure it.
Having seen the entire land as far as the ocean and having observed out of curiosity the royal courts of the kings, he has now returned once more to his own country;
thus, out of compassion for young people and through the entreaties of the virtuous, this *Mugdhopadeśa* (Instruction for the Simple) has been composed by the poet Jalhaṇa.
Childhood was made fruitful through familiarity with the succession of studies in the sciences; youth was honored by the constant embraces of young women;
and now, on the banks of the celestial river, a remaining duty remains for us to bring about the purity of our old age through sincere worship of Śambhu.
